title: Rome: unwritten tradition is natural — Jews, pagan states, Pythagoras and Socrates
source_text: XXVI. Praeterea Pontificii, traditiones non scriptas necessarias esse probant ex more omnium gentium. Nam primo, inquiunt, Judaei traditiones aliquas extra Scripturam habuerunt, & etiamnum habent. Deinde omnes profanae Respublicae magna ex parte legibus non scriptis reguntur, ut olim Athenienses, & Lacedaemonii, & etiam antiqui Galli, sicut testantur Caesar, Thucydides, & Plutarchus. Ac praeterea Philosophi nobilissimi & celeberrimi, Pythagoras & Socrates, cum plurima docuerint, nihil tamen scripserunt. Unde concludit Bellarminus naturam ipsam quodammodo clamare traditiones non scriptas necessarias, vel certe utilissimas esse.
pass_a_gloss: Besides, the Pontificians prove that unwritten traditions are necessary from the custom of all nations. For first, they say, the Jews have had some traditions outside Scripture, and still have them. Then all profane Republics are for the most part ruled by unwritten laws, as once the Athenians, and the Lacedaemonians, and also the ancient Gauls, as Caesar, Thucydides, and Plutarch testify. And besides the most noble and celebrated Philosophers, Pythagoras and Socrates, though they taught very many things, yet wrote nothing. Whence Bellarmine concludes that nature itself in a way cries out that unwritten traditions are necessary, or at least most useful.
pass_b_english: Next Rome proof: every nation runs on unwritten custom.
Jews keep extra-scriptural traditions; Athens, Sparta, and the Gauls used unwritten law.
Pythagoras and Socrates taught much and wrote nothing.
Bellarmine: nature itself cries that unwritten tradition is necessary or most useful.
